books.section: America in an Era of Turmoil (1960-1975)

source: original; stimulus table compiled from the Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3, and the Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, Table 539.
stimulus.text:
Federal spending, 1950-1980 (Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3; defense shares from the Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, Table 539, using Office of Management and Budget figures):

| Fiscal year | Federal outlays as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) | Defense as a share of all federal outlays |
| 1950 | 15.6% | 32% |
| 1960 | 17.8% | 52% |
| 1970 | 19.3% | 42% |
| 1980 | 21.7% | 23% |

stem: Federal outlays grew as a share of the economy while defense took a smaller share of them. Which of the following best explains that combination?

options.text: The government spent less money in total by 1980 than it had spent in 1950.
options.misconception: The first column shows outlays taking a larger share of the economy in 1980, not a smaller one.

options.text: The government cut all domestic programs to pay for a much bigger defense budget instead.
options.misconception: If domestic programs had been cut, the defense share would have risen, but the table shows it falling from 52 percent to 23 percent.

options.text: Defense spending disappeared entirely by 1980, so the military received nothing at all that year.
options.misconception: The table still gives defense 23 percent of all outlays in 1980.

options.text: Domestic programs grew faster than defense, so the government grew as defense shrank as a share.

rationales.A: The first column shows outlays taking a larger share of the economy in 1980, not a smaller one.
rationales.B: If domestic programs had been cut, the defense share would have risen, but the table shows it falling from 52 percent to 23 percent.
rationales.C: The table still gives defense 23 percent of all outlays in 1980.
rationales.D: Background: Medicare, Social Security, and other domestic programs grew in the 1960s and 1970s, while defense spending fell as a share after the Vietnam War.
rationales.general:
1. The two columns move in opposite directions after 1960: the total share rises while the defense share falls.
2. If defense took a smaller share of a bigger total, something else must have grown faster than defense.
3. Background: That something else was domestic spending, including Social Security, Medicare, and Great Society programs.
4. The table alone cannot name the programs, but the direction of the two columns rules out the other answers.
Remember: When two columns move in opposite directions, ask what grew to fill the gap.
